description: Project Lunyx will take on the Lunar Landing Site Navigator track for NASA Space Apps 2026.
summary:
Welcome to Lunyx, an interactive 3D web app for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. Pick a site on the Moon, choose an arrival date, and step onto the surface to see when the Sun and Earth are visible above the local terrain. Near the lunar south pole, ridges and crater rims can block the low Sun or hide Earth from view, affecting when a lander can use solar power or communicate directly with Earth.
Lunyx lets users compare landing sites, arrival times, and mast heights to see how those choices affect sunlight, darkness, and Earth visibility. It helps mission planners shortlist sites and dates for further study and gives students and educators an interactive way to explore the same decisions.
details:
• Globe view. A 3D Moon with real relief from the LOLA whole-Moon grid, drawn at true scale, 28 catalogued landings and a pin anywhere. Filters: UTC date and time, the latitude and longitude at the centre of the view, the required solar elevation band, mast height, mission window and arrival delay, "Missions to replay" (see Run it) and "Go to a landing site", a list that also works from the keyboard: choosing a landing opens its card, and a double-click goes down to its surface view. Overlays with legends: where the Sun is inside the elevation band (smooth Moon), long-term average sunlight and Earth visibility (NASA PGDA product 69, polar regions only), elevation-data coverage and mapped ice-bearing shadowed regions. A compass, a locator map and a mission-window time scrubber that draws each sunrise and sunset from its start to its end, with jumps to either end. Landing markers are coloured by the country their hardware belongs to, with optional flags, and an optional tint of the whole Moon by the country of the nearest landing shown (the "Show country territories" switch in Filters, off by default: a display of who landed nearest, not of ownership; see Known limits). The site card shows who owns the hardware (from the GCAT catalogue), the area explored at the site, the data behind the site, the Sun and Earth against its skyline with both ends of their next rise or set, the mission window's sunlight and Earth in view (by Earth's centre and by any part of its disc), and a site-science section: Deep Space Network station opportunities, long-term averages, the nearest mapped ice targets, Diviner annual maximum and mean temperature, and ShadowCam mosaics as links.
  • Surface view. Stand at the site and look around: black sky, terrain drawn from the elevation data out to 246 km, the Sun and Earth at their computed positions and sizes, Earth's phase, terrain shadows and both bodies' tracks. Key metrics (upper left): Sun and Earth position and clearance above the skyline now, countdowns to the next sunset, sunrise, Earthset and Earthrise (to whichever end of each comes next, with both ends below it), the mission-window figures with Earth by its centre and by any part of its disc, and where the numbers come from. A skyline chart (lower left) with the Sun's and Earth's samples over the window, a time mode that marks each rise and set as a band, and a table. An explanation of what hides the Sun or Earth at a given instant. The control strip is one row: "Track Sun" and "Track Earth", which keep the view turned to that body as the clock runs (dragging or the arrow keys stop it), "Surface options" (Sky paths, Generated detail, Skyline chart, Return to site) and "About" (the status, ground-data and owner lines). In the surface view every panel (key metrics, skyline chart, surface controls, time, locator map, compare, assistant) has a handle to move it, with the mouse or the arrow keys, and a Fold button; "Reset panels" puts them back, the assistant can move, fold and reset them too, and leaving the surface view restores the usual layout. The initial mission window is 29.5 days; chosen windows and mission presets keep their own durations. The surface locator map shows your walking position as a yellow dot and the landing site as an outlined square, with its own zoom for viewing local movement.
  • Compare panel. Scenarios A and B side by side with B minus A in numbers and sentences; "B = A arriving N hours later"; "B = A with another mast"; named comparisons that reload exactly. Nearby alternatives: a scan around the site (radius, spacing, slope limit) ranked by sunlight and Earth contact, any candidate taken as B. The mission-window table (every sunlit, dark and Earth-in-view spell, and every rise and set with both ends), downloadable as CSV or JSON. The seasonal outlook: sunlight and Earth in view (by its centre and by any part of its disc) for each lunar day over the coming months, as a chart and a table.
  • Assistant. A drawer (button lower right) where you ask in words; "Close ×" or Escape closes it without leaving the surface view. It operates the app through the same actions as the on-screen controls and lists what it ran. Without Claude credentials it answers in a labelled deterministic mode (see The assistant).
